title: Stellar nursery in the arms of NGC 1672
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1672, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1672 · constellation Dorado · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #44 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Clusters of hot young blue stars line the spiral arms of this galaxy, while clouds of hydrogen gas glow red and thin curtains of dust dim and redden the stars behind them. This is NGC 1672, a barred spiral about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Dorado, photographed by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

Its balanced, symmetric look comes from four principal arms, each edged by prominent dust lanes that reach out from the center. A barred spiral has a straight band of stars across its middle, and the arms extend from its ends.

The colors trace star birth. Blue marks young, hot stars that formed recently, and the red glow comes from hydrogen gas in the regions where stars are being made. Dust makes starlight look redder as it passes through, because the grains scatter blue light more than red, so the dust lanes both hide and tint what lies behind them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.42 x 3.17 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 77,000 × 55,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and red filters. The caption describes young stars as blue and hydrogen gas as red, but the per-filter color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures collect far more light than the eye can, revealing faint dust and gas.
